name: Earplugs
summary: Plugs that seal the ear canal to cut noise: roll-down foam, pre-moulded flanged plugs, plugs on a band (canal caps) and custom moulds.
uses: Engines, generators, chainsaws, grinders and saws: a good fit cuts the noise a lot, but always less than the number on the box
At 100 dBA and up, or for sudden loud bangs, NIOSH says wear muffs over plugs; CCOHS counts the pair as only 5 dB better than the higher rating (NIOSH bulletin; CCOHS hearing)
Only works while it's in: taking it out for 5 minutes in an hour cuts a 25 dB plug to no more than 11 dB (CCOHS hearing)
Too much protection hides alarms, shouts and the sound of your own machine; aim to hear voices, not the roar
Swim plugs, hearing-aid moulds and earbuds are not hearing protection, however snug they feel
identify: Foam plugs are rolled thin and expand in the canal; pre-moulded plugs are shaped to fit; canal caps sit on a light band (NIOSH hearing PPE). US packs must show an NRR (noise reduction rating) in decibels under the EPA label rule (OSHA OTM). Canadian packs may also show a class under CSA Z94.2: A for about 95–105 dBA, B 90–95, C below 90; above 105 dBA use plugs and muffs together (WorkSafeBC hearing; WorkplaceNL hearing). European plugs fall under EN 352-2, should carry the CE mark, and are chosen by their SNR and H, M, L values (DIN EN 352-2; uvex EN 352; OSHWIKI hearing). The label is a lab number and real wearers get much less. OSHA takes 7 dB off the NRR for dBA readings and, to judge engineering controls, halves what is left; NIOSH takes 50% off formable foam plugs and about 70 to 75% off other plugs (70% in one place, 75% in another); CSA Z94.2 uses half the NRR; HSE assumes 4 dB more noise at the ear than the test predicts (OSHA OTM; NIOSH 98-126; CCOHS hearing; HSE real world). So an NRR 32 foam plug may give roughly 9 to 13 dB. A pack with no NRR, SNR or class has not been rated: treat it as unknown. Musicians' flat-response plugs are real protectors too (NIOSH hearing PPE).
test: Foam: it should be soft, pliable and clean. Throw out plugs that are hard, torn or dirty; disposable foam can't be washed and must be thrown away once soiled (Moldex 6985; CCOHS hearing; HSE hearing protection). Check any plug for wear or tear before each use (EC hearing protection). Fit with clean hands: it takes practice to straighten the ear canal (HSE press 2025); the steps are roll, pull, hold (NIOSH earplugs). Roll the plug into a thin snake. Pull the top of your ear up and back with your opposite hand to straighten the canal. Slide the plug in and hold it with a fingertip until the foam has swelled to fill the canal (NIOSH earplugs). Most of the foam should be deep in the canal, not sticking out. Your voice sounds muffled when the plug has sealed. Then cup your hands tightly over your ears: if it gets much quieter, the plug may not be sealing, so take it out and try again (NIOSH earplugs; NIOSH bulletin). Poor fit and wrong insertion are big reasons people get less than the label (CCOHS hearing; HSE real world).

decay.note: Estimate. Moldex's own use-by dates are 5 years for most of its hearing protection and 1 year for its Soothers foam plugs, and no US or Canadian rule sets them. Used foam plugs get dirty and are thrown away; replace plugs that stop being pliable.

improvise: Real earplugs or earmuffs are the only reliable protection. Without them, get away from the noise or cut your time near it: removing the person from the noise is the first fix (NIOSH 98-126). For a short emergency, fingers pushed firmly into the ear canals give about 25–30 dB, enough for a brief blast but no use while you work (Berger 2006). Cotton gives only about 5–10 dB except at the highest pitches, and cigarette filters give no protection below 500 Hz (Berger 2006); NIOSH says cotton, cigarette filters and similar items should not be used in place of hearing protectors (NIOSH 98-126). Earbuds, headphones, swim plugs and hearing-aid moulds are not protection (NIOSH 98-126). In a shortage, keep a foam plug only while it is still clean, soft and pliable (HSE hearing protection; CCOHS hearing); Moldex says disposable foam can't be washed and must be thrown away once soiled (Moldex 6985). NIOSH says to wear muffs over plugs at 100 dBA and above, as with chainsaws and jackhammers (NIOSH bulletin).
